rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Adam may derive from adīm, the earth's surface; a hadith links this to Adam's earthly origin and humanity's varied colors, temperaments, and fortunes.
rows.anchor: Some derive Adam from adīm, meaning the surface of the earth, in keeping with the ḥadīth,

rows.speaker: Ibn ʿAbbās
rows.claim: The names taught to Adam are ordinary words people use with one another, including man, sea, mountain, and kettle.
rows.anchor: such as Ibn ʿAbbās, to be those that people use in discourse with one another, such as “man,” “sea,”“mountain,” and even “kettle.”

rows.speaker: Mujāhid
rows.claim: Adam was taught the names of everything.
rows.anchor: To others, such as Mujāhid, they are “the names of everything.”

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Adam was taught the names of the angels.
rows.anchor: Still others say he was taught the names of angels;

rows.speaker: al-Ṭabarī
rows.claim: Adam was taught the names of all his progeny; al-Ṭabarī favors this because the pronoun hum suggests named humans or angels.
rows.anchor: or that he was taught the names of all his progeny, which the commentator al-Ṭabarī prefers, in part because the pronoun hum is used rather than hāʾ,

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The masculine plural pronoun usually refers to human or angelic persons, while nonpersons usually take a feminine singular pronoun, though 24:45 is an exception.
rows.anchor: The plural of persons (human beings and angels) is the masculine plural, but the plural of other things (animals, inanimate objects) is usually expressed by the feminine singular pronoun, though this rule does not always hold

rows.speaker: al-Rāzī
rows.claim: Adam learned all earthly languages, and his descendants gradually came to prefer one language over the others.
rows.anchor: For al-Rāzī, this means that Adam indeed was taught all the languages of the earth, and his descendants came to prefer one over the others in the course of time.

rows.speaker: al-Ṭabrisī
rows.claim: A comparable process of linguistic differentiation would have followed the flood.
rows.anchor: The commentator al-ṭabrisī adds that a similar process would have taken place after the flood.

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: “Laid them before” can refer either to the names themselves or to the objects those names designate.
rows.anchor: Laid them before refers either to the names themselves or to the objects named.

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Being taught the names of things can mean being granted knowledge of all things.
rows.anchor: For some, to be taught the names of things means to be given knowledge of all things.

rows.speaker: Ibn ʿArabī
rows.claim: Ibn ʿArabī analogizes the angels' diverse functions and hierarchy to human spiritual and sensory faculties, each limited and unable to perceive what is above itself.
rows.anchor: Ibn ʿArabī’s interpretation of this passage begins by pointing out that in relation to the world angels “are like the spiritual and sensory faculties” in human beings.

rows.speaker: Ibn ʿArabī
rows.claim: Adam's synthetic reality let him know all the Divine Names; the angels lacked that synthesis and could not glorify God through Names they did not know, so Adam knew God in ways they could not.
rows.anchor: Adam was capable of knowing all the Divine Names, unlike the angels who “did not possess the synthesis possessed by Adam, and were not aware of the Divine Names

rows.speaker: commentators
rows.claim: The Blessing is commonly understood as deliverance from Pharaoh, followed by manna, quails, and the promised land.
rows.anchor: The Blessing (niʿmah; see also vv. 47, 122) is usually understood to be the deliverance from Pharaoh (vv. 49–50) and the subsequent heavenly gifts of manna, quails, and the promised land;

rows.speaker: commentators
rows.claim: Another interpretation identifies the Blessing as God's placing prophets among the Israelites and sending them Divine books.
rows.anchor: or that God placed prophets among them and sent them Divine books;

rows.speaker: commentators
rows.claim: Some understand the Blessing as Islam's coming, since the verse addresses Jews living in and around Madinah.
rows.anchor: or the coming of Islam, since this verse addresses the Jews in and around Madinah.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Niʿmah can also have its broadest sense, beginning with creation, consistent with the universal commands that follow.
rows.anchor: Niʿmah is understood in the most general sense as well, beginning with the gift of creation, in keeping with the universal commands of the following verses.

rows.speaker: commentators
rows.claim: The covenant can broadly mean the people's gratitude and, on God's side, His forgiveness and reward.
rows.anchor: which is understood broadly as people’s gratitude, on the one hand, and God’s Forgiveness and Reward, on the other.

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: The covenant may be the pact in 5:12, in which God made a covenant with Israel and raised twelve chieftains among them.
rows.anchor: Another interpretation is that it refers to the mīthāq (“covenant” or “pact”) of 5:12: God had made a covenant with the Children of Israel, and We raised among them twelve chieftains.

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: The covenant may require fidelity to the foretold coming of the Prophet, described in the Torah and Gospel available to them.
rows.anchor: Some interpret it to mean that they should be true to the predicted coming of the Prophet, whom they find inscribed in the Torah and the Gospel that is with them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This verse echoes 2:153; the Qurʾān also links patience with steadfastness in hardship and good through 12:18, 16:127, 23:111, 70:5, 90:17, and 103:3.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṣabr means both enduring hardship and remaining steadfast in good.
rows.anchor: ṣabr, like “patience,” means both the endurance of hardship and steadfastness in good.

rows.speaker: commentators
rows.claim: The pronoun translated “this” may refer to prayer alone or to the whole admonition; the matter is difficult because it demands attention by day and night.
rows.anchor: This—translating a pronoun denoting prayer or the admonition as a whole (IK)—is difficult

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Patience can be practiced through deferred gratification, whereas prayer requires retreating from the world and diminishing the ego.
rows.anchor: one can be patient through the commonplace discipline of deferred gratification, whereas prayer always demands, in some measure, a retreat from the world and a diminution of the ego.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Numbers 11:4–5 parallels Israel's craving for foods remembered from Egypt, including cucumbers, onions, and garlic.
rows.anchor: A Biblical parallel to this verse’s content is found in Numbers 11:4–5, where the Israelites crave meat and wish for the “fish . . . the cucumbers, the

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Numbers 11:31–35 says quails were given, but those who craved them were struck down for greed toward God's provision.
rows.anchor: In Numbers 11:31–35, they are given quails, only to have those who craved them struck down for their greediness in relation to God’s provision.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word fūm, rendered garlic, may instead mean wheat.
rows.anchor: Here garlic ( fūm ) may also mean “wheat.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Habaṭa, “go down,” need not describe a change in elevation; English similarly uses “descend” for arriving at a place or moving into or out of a valley.
rows.anchor: need not be a change in elevation; analogously, in English one might say that one “descends” upon a place;

rows.speaker: commentators
rows.claim: The better food refers to manna and quails, while the lesser food means the items the Israelites requested.
rows.anchor: Better is usually understood here to refer to the manna and quails, while the lesser refers to the other foods they were requesting.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Miṣr can mean a town or city; as a proper name or foreign word, it means Egypt.
rows.anchor: A town renders miṣr, which can also mean a city, and used as a proper name or foreign word it means “Egypt.”

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: The orthography requires miṣran rather than miṣra and therefore excludes Egypt itself; some early commentators nevertheless understood it as Pharaoh's miṣr.
rows.anchor: though some mention is made of early commentators understanding this to be the “miṣr of Pharaoh.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The killing of prophets recurs in Qurʾānic passages and has parallels in Luke, Matthew, Romans, 1 Thessalonians, and 1 Kings.
rows.anchor: The killing of the prophets (2:61, 87, 91; 3:21, 112, 181; 4:155; 5:70) is also mentioned several times in the Bible (Luke 13:34; Matthew 23:37; Romans 11:3; 1 Thessalonians 2:14–15; 1 Kings 19:10).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse recalls the qiblah discussion at 2:115c: East and West belong to God.
rows.anchor: See 2:115c, which discusses the qiblah and how the East and the West belong to God.

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: The future “will say” can describe a recurring trait in the past, not only predict a future objection.
rows.anchor: The use of the future will say in this verse does not exclude its referring to the past, as a kind of trait, and not only a prediction (R).

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: The prayer direction is not inherently merited by Jerusalem or Makkah; its authority comes from God's command.
rows.anchor: The verse is meant partly to remind one that it is not the place itself (Jerusalem or Makkah) that merits being the direction of prayer or qiblah, but the fact that God has commanded it to be so (R).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After the Hijrah the Prophet faced Jerusalem for between thirteen and twenty months; most reports give sixteen or seventeen.
rows.anchor: in the reports the number of months varies between thirteen and twenty, but most mention sixteen or seventeen (IK, Q, Ṭ).

rows.speaker: some accounts
rows.claim: Some accounts say the Prophet and followers faced the Kaʿbah in Makkah, then Jerusalem briefly after migration, then the Kaʿbah again; others say they faced Jerusalem even in Makkah.
rows.anchor: Some accounts state that, initially, the Prophet and his followers, while still in Makkah, prayed in the direction of the Kaʿbah, then faced Jerusalem for a brief period after migrating to Madinah, and then faced the Kaʿbah once more. Others aver, however, that even while in Makkah they prayed toward Jerusalem

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Some commentators say hypocrites posed the question about the new qiblah cynically and without sincerity.
rows.anchor: Some commentators believe that it was the hypocrites who asked this question regarding the change in direction and that, as such, they were not sincere but cynical in their intentions (Ṭ).

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: The qiblah change is the first chronological case of Qurʾānic abrogation and a paradigm in which the Qurʾān abrogates Sunnah; see 2:106c.
rows.anchor: It is the first instance of abrogation in the chronological order of revelation and is often cited as a paradigmatic case, though it is an instance of the Quran abrogating the Sunnah (Q); on naskh, see 2:106c.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The mosque of the Two Qiblahs is associated with a report that an announcement of the change came during prayer and the congregation turned mid-prayer.
rows.anchor: it was reported that in the midst of a prayer, a caller came to announce the change in direction, at which the congregation turned, mid-prayer, and faced the new qiblah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Determining the qiblah outside Makkah has long generated debate and several methods.
rows.anchor: Determining the qiblah in locales outside of Makkah has been and continues to be a subject of lively debate. Several different methods have been employed throughout the centuries

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One early method divided the world into sectors oriented toward extended Kaʿbah walls; cardinal directions and markers such as summer sunrise and Canopus helped determine prayer direction.
rows.anchor: One early method was to stand as though one were facing a wall of the Kaʿbah that was extended far enough horizontally; in this system the Islamic world was divided into geographic sectors

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The great-circle route is the shortest surface path; in North America it begins northeast and curves toward southeast, while the older sector method points southeast, and both are used today.
rows.anchor: among them the great circle, which is the shortest surface line between Makkah and any spot on the earth. In North America, for example, the great circle to Makkah begins in a northeasterly direction

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another method keeps a constant compass bearing, or rhumb line, toward Makkah.
rows.anchor: Another method is to face the direction that, if one kept a constant compass bearing or “rhumb line,” would bring one to Makkah.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Older mosques could point in different directions because of nonmathematical local methods; Islamic mathematics later used instruments and sometimes prompted wall adjustments.
rows.anchor: In some old Islamic cities the qiblah of various mosques was not always uniformly oriented, because it was calculated using the nonmathematical means available to their inhabitants.

rows.speaker: aḥādith
rows.claim: A hadith says the area between East and West is a qiblah; it is read as allowing latitude on precision when calculation or local conditions make exact direction difficult or impossible.
rows.anchor: Aḥadith states, “Whatever is between the east and the west is a qiblah” (IK, Q), which has been interpreted as providing a certain latitude when it comes to matters of exact direction,

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: The opening “thus” links the verse to what precedes: as the Kaʿbah is earth's center, the community is middle, or as God guided the community, He made it middle.
rows.anchor: The thus at the start of this verse is thought to connect this verse to what precedes it, so that it is saying, “Just as the Kaʿbah is the center of the earth, so too are you the middle people,”

rows.speaker: the Prophet
rows.claim: A hadith glosses middle as just.
rows.anchor: According to a ḥadīth, the Prophet said that middle means “just,”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A proverb, treated as a hadith by some, says the best things are middlemost; calling someone a people's middlemost means esteemed, perhaps because people gather around their leader.
rows.anchor: and a proverb (considered a ḥadīth by some) states,“The best of things is their middlemost.” When one says that a man is the middlemost of his people, it means he is among their best and most esteemed people

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: In idiomatic Arabic, wasaṭ, “middle,” often means the choicest part of something.
rows.anchor: In idiomatic Arabic, often the wasaṭ (“middle”) of a thing is the choicest part (R).

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: In faith and practice, being middle means avoiding extremes; courage and generosity each occupy a virtuous mean between opposing vices.
rows.anchor: With regard to faith and practice, to be in the middle means to avoid extremes (R): the virtue of courage lies between recklessness and cowardice, and the virtue of generosity lies between prodigality and miserliness

rows.speaker: Āl
rows.claim: “Middle” can describe Muslims' position among other religious communities.
rows.anchor: It can also mean that Muslims are in the middle in relation to other communities (Āl).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Muslim writers describe Islam as balancing Judaism's emphasis on law with Christianity's emphasis on love and mercy, and as balancing exoteric with esoteric concerns.
rows.anchor: Muslims have argued that while Judaism emphasizes the law and Christianity emphasizes love and mercy, Islam creates a balance between the two or between emphasis on the exoteric and the esoteric;

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islam also balances worldly concerns with the demands of the Hereafter, and its middle position can refer to geography.
rows.anchor: Islam also creates a balance between the concerns of this world and the demands of the Hereafter. At another level, many have pointed to the geographical location of Islam in the middle belt of the world.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Witnessing entails a consequential role in judging through knowledge; 36:65 pictures the body testifying against the soul on Judgment Day.
rows.anchor: To be a witness means one has a consequential role in the judging of a thing through one’s knowledge of that thing. Thus in 36:65 God warns,

rows.speaker: the Prophet
rows.claim: A hadith says God admits a Muslim to the Garden when four witnesses testify for that person; the number is successively reduced to three and two, and ʿUmar declines to ask about one.
rows.anchor: The commentators often mention a ḥadīth in which the Prophet said, “God will cause to enter the Garden any Muslim for whom four people bear witness.”

rows.speaker: the Prophet
rows.claim: The Prophet told the community that it is God's witness over mankind.
rows.anchor: Similarly, the Prophet said,“You are God’s witnesses over mankind.”

rows.speaker: the Prophet
rows.claim: Hadiths describe Muhammad's community testifying on Judgment Day that other prophets fulfilled their missions, even when their own peoples deny them.
rows.anchor: The commentators specifically mention various aḥādīth in which, on the Day of Judgment, the community of Muhammad will testify to other prophets’ faithfulness to their missions, even when those prophets’ own people do not (IK);

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: Shāhid or shahīd can mean testimony, testament, or evidence; a witness is both one who testifies and someone who is witnessed.
rows.anchor: A shāhid or shahīd can also be a testimony or testament to something, evidence of something (R)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Read as living evidence, the Prophet testifies to his community while the Muslim community guides humanity toward knowledge of God and truth; 22:78 supports this reading.
rows.anchor: the Prophet is evidence or testimony for his community to look to, and in relation to the other communities of the world the Islamic community is a testimony or evidence of something for the sake of other communities

rows.speaker: al-Ṭabarī
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabarī says hypocrites objected that Muhammad's community had changed its qiblah.
rows.anchor: According to al-Ṭabarī, the hypocrites objected to the change in the qiblah by saying, “What is wrong with you, that you have a qiblah, then you change it?”

rows.speaker: al-Ṭabarī
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabarī reports Jews argued that Muhammad longed for home and might have been the awaited Prophet had he kept their qiblah.
rows.anchor: The Jews said, “Muhammad longs for his homeland, but had he remained with our qiblah, we would have considered him the one we were waiting for.”

rows.speaker: al-Ṭabarī
rows.claim: Al-Ṭabarī reports Makkan idolaters accused Muhammad of wavering in his religion.
rows.anchor: The Makkan idolaters said, “Muhammad has wavered in his religion.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The statement that God would not let the believers' faith be in vain reassures those who prayed toward Jerusalem and died before the change.
rows.anchor: some commentators see God would not let your belief be in vain as a reassurance for those who faced the Jerusalem qiblah, but died before it was changed

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: “So that We observe” interprets “in order that We may know” while preserving God's eternal knowledge: observation concerns what exists, while God knows before it exists.
rows.anchor: Some interpret this to mean, “So that We observe,” which would preserve the principle that God’s Knowledge is eternal; that is, one could only observe a thing that exists, while God could know it before it exists

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: Another interpretation says “so that My friends and partisans will know,” treating followers' acts as attributable to their leader, as in the saying that ʿUmar conquered Jerusalem.
rows.anchor: Some interpret it to mean, “So that My friends and partisans will know,” reasoning that the actions of one’s followers can be attributed to their leader, as when one says, “ʿUmar conquered Jerusalem,”

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: A third interpretation is “so that you will all know,” addressing Muslims and opponents; the divine first person softens the condemnation of disbelief.
rows.anchor: It can also mean, “So that you will all know,” referring to both Muslims and their opponents, where the use of the grammatical first person conveys a sense of kindness;

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The issue resembles Qurʾānic tests such as 29:2: God already knows the answer, yet a trial and its outcome still occur; this raises a central problem about eternal knowledge and a changing world.
rows.anchor: According to Islamic theology, although God tests in order to know, He does not wait for the answer. The answer is known already in His eternal Knowledge, but the trial and its outcome still actually take place.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This verse echoes 2:45; 3:200 calls believers to vie in patience, while 90:17 and 103:3 call them to exhort one another to it.
rows.anchor: Recourse to patience and prayer is also mentioned in v. 45, and 3:200 enjoins believers to vie in patience, while 90:17 and 103:3 enjoin them to exhort one another to patience

rows.speaker: commentators
rows.claim: Commentators divide patience into avoiding sins, persisting in meritorious acts, and accepting affliction.
rows.anchor: Commentators usually categorize patience into three kinds: being resolute in avoiding sins, constant in meritorious actions, and content in the face of affliction

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God is described as being with the patient also in 8:46, 8:66, 2:177, 3:142, 22:35, and 39:10.
rows.anchor: God is also referred to as being with the patient in 8:46, 66; see also 2:177; 3:142; 22:35; 39:10.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This is among the Qurʾān's most frequently recited verses.
rows.anchor: This is one of the most often recited verses of the Quran.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Each of the verse's three instances uses ilāh, the general word for god or divinity, rather than Allāh, God's supreme personal Name in Arabic.
rows.anchor: In all three instances in this verse God renders ilāh, the general noun for “god” or “divinity,”rather than Allāh, which is the supreme personal Name of God in Arabic.

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: Wāḥid means one and includes uniqueness, indivisibility, and having no equal or likeness.
rows.anchor: which includes the sense of being unique, not made up of parts, without equal or like (Ṭ).
